text:
Michael: Quick RFC follow-up: we need to pick an approach for the private control plane in customer VPCs. Two candidates: 1) sidecar-in-vpc agent that owns TLS and local egress, or 2) peered central control plane (PrivateLink/peering) with lightweight agents. Thoughts?

Jess: Sidecar keeps control traffic inside customer network which helps compliance and egress-IP preservation. Ops cost is higher though: upgrades, CA rotation distribution, health of many agents.

Tom: Peered central CP simplifies rollout and global visibility. Downsides: peering/privateLink complexity, cross-account networking, and a larger blast radius on CP outages.

Carol: Auth handshake is a major variable. Sidecar allows mTLS with local key material. Peering we'd probably do signed tokens or short-lived certs -- need to avoid exposing customer KMS.

Kevin: Spike idea: signed attestation tokens. Flow: CP issues nonce, sidecar proves key possession via temp cert signed by CP-bound CA. Lower network churn than full mutual TLS each time.

Maria: Rotation/lifecycle: how do we rotate sidecar CA and keys for on-prem or air-gapped installs? Pull model won't always work. We need operator tooling or well-defined manual rotation paths.

SRE-bot: perf-note: peering adds ~1-2ms median to control RPCs; sidecar placement variability adds 0-5ms depending on subnet and AZ.

Jess: Failure modes: peered CP outage => many customers impacted. We need degraded-mode behavior: cache last-known config locally, allow read-only ops until reconnection.

Tom: Egress-IP preservation: sidecar naturally preserves customer source IPs which matters for allowlists. Peering can preserve if NAT stays on customer side, but then CP loses source-level metrics.

Carol: Hybrid pattern proposal: primary peered-CP for control plane, plus a minimal agent that only handles egress IP pinning, local secret material, and token caching. Keeps agent surface small.

Kevin: Security: token model must include nonce+ttl and tenant binding. Add replay protection and revocation endpoint. Also bind tokens to SNI/x-tenant-id to prevent cross-tenant reuse.

Maria: Experiment plan: implement token-handshake prototype in cp-proto branch. Add runtime flag `cp_handshake_mode={peered,agent-hybrid}`. Canary two consenting customers for 72h. Measure: handshake_success_rate, cp_lag_ms, token_replay_attempts, cert_rotation_latency.

Jess: I'll draft the canary runbook (checkpoints, rollback criteria, dashboard links). Carol can handle customer opt-in.

Carol: I can own the canary and the runbook updates. Will request 2 non-production tenants and a rollback route to agent-local mode.

Deploy-bot: Deploy queued: cp-proto/token-handshake -> staging (canary: az-1).

Michael: If we see frequent replay or token failures, fallback to mTLS for affected tenants and capture detailed audit logs. Also retain logs for 30d for compliance.

Tom: Long-term consideration: if fleet-managed agent updates + attestation become reliable, sidecar operational cost drops and agent-first becomes attractive again.

Kevin: I'll write the RFC follow-up doc with diagrams, security checks, and PR links. ETA: EOD.

SRE-bot: note: thread archived automatically after 14d of inactivity.
